--- title: "Training error and the error on new data" description: "A model's error on the stations it was fitted to says little about new sites: five models ranked by it come out nearly upside down, and the gap depends on the model and on the amount of data." order: 1 categories: [generalisation] --- ## Training error flatters a model Every fitted model can report its error on the data it was fitted to. That number comes free, and it is easy to read as a measure of how good the model is. This page shows that it is a poor guide to how a model will do on new sites, and that the more flexible the model, the poorer the guide. Five models from [section 3](../03-supervised-learning/index.qmd), ranked by that number, come out nearly upside down. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Training error and the error on new data The **training error** is a model's error on the examples it was fitted to. The **error on new data** is its error on examples it has never seen, and it is the one that matters: a model is fitted to be used on new data. Data hold two kinds of pattern. **Signal** is the part that will appear again in new data, such as warmer water holding more of a species. **Noise** is the part peculiar to the examples at hand: a lucky haul, a sensor reading slightly off. A model cannot tell the two apart, and fitting noise lowers the training error just as fitting signal does. But only the signal carries over to new data. So the training error is usually lower than the error on new data, and the difference between them is called the **optimism**. A rigid model, such as a straight line, has little room to fit noise, so its two errors stay close. A flexible model can bend through every training example, so its training error can fall to zero while its error on new data does not. More data shrinks the optimism, since noise in many examples is harder to fit than noise in a few. ::: {.diagram} ![A rigid model misses training and new data by about as much. A flexible model passes through every training point, so its training error is zero, but it misses new data by more.](img/training-and-new-error.svg){fig-alt="Two cards, each showing the same nine training points and four new points. A rigid model, a straight line: it misses the training points and the new points by about as much, and two bars, training error and error on new data, are about the same length. A flexible model, bending through every point: its training error bar is empty and its error on new data bar is the longest. A note says the gap between the two errors grows with flexibility and shrinks with more data."} ::: ## Worked example The data and the split by site are those of [Decision trees](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd): three quarters of the monitoring sites for training and a quarter held back as test sites. This page uses only the training sites; the test sites are kept for the end of the section. Each model is fitted to some of the training sites and scored on the rest, which play the part of new sites. One such split leaves only a few dozen sites to score on, and by chance they can be easier or harder to predict than the others. So the training sites are split 20 times at random, by site, three quarters for fitting and a quarter as new sites, and each error is averaged over the 20 splits. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) # 20 random splits of the training sites: fitting sites and new sites splits <- group_mc_cv(train, group = site_id, prop = 0.75, times = 20) predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season tree_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) boost_recipe <- tree_recipe |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) c(training_sites = n_distinct(train$site_id), splits = nrow(splits)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> training_sites splits #> 120 20 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor, RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, PolynomialFeatures from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train = survey.iloc[train_rows] # scikit-learn's models need numbers, so one recipe serves all five. tree_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) # 20 random splits of the training sites: fitting sites and new sites splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=20, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) splits = list(splitter.split(train, groups=train["site_id"])) {"training_sites": train["site_id"].nunique(), "splits": len(splits)} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> {'training_sites': 120, 'splits': 20} ``` ::: ::: ::: ### Each model scored on its own stations and on new sites The five models run from rigid to flexible: linear regression; a decision tree three questions deep; a decision tree grown out until each leaf holds a single station; a random forest of 500 trees; and boosting with 500 trees, each six questions deep. The boosted model is deliberately large, so that it has room to fit the noise. Each is fitted to the fitting sites of every split and scored twice, on the stations it was fitted to and on the new sites. Predicting the fitting stations' average count everywhere, with no inputs at all, gives a baseline. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tree_model <- function(depth) { decision_tree(mode = "regression", tree_depth = depth, min_n = 2, cost_complexity = 0) } forest_model <- rand_forest(mode = "regression", trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) boost_model <- boost_tree(mode = "regression", trees = 500, tree_depth = 6, learn_rate = 0.1) models <- list( "Linear regression" = workflow(tree_recipe, linear_reg()), "Decision tree, depth 3" = workflow(tree_recipe, tree_model(3)), "Decision tree, grown out" = workflow(tree_recipe, tree_model(30)), "Random forest" = workflow(tree_recipe, forest_model), "Boosting" = workflow(boost_recipe, boost_model) ) score_split <- function(s) { fitting <- analysis(s) new <- assessment(s) imap(models, \(w, model) { fitted <- fit(w, fitting) tibble(model = model, training = rmse_vec(fitting$abundance, predict(fitted, fitting)$.pred), new = rmse_vec(new$abundance, predict(fitted, new)$.pred), # ranger's out-of-bag error, used further down oob = if (model == "Random forest") sqrt(extract_fit_engine(fitted)$prediction.error) else NA) }) |> list_rbind() |> add_row(model = "Predict the average", training = NA, new = rmse_vec(new$abundance, rep(mean(fitting$abundance), nrow(new)))) } scores <- map(splits$splits, score_split) |> list_rbind() results <- scores |> group_by(model) |> summarise(across(c(training, new, oob), mean)) |> mutate(optimism = new - training) |> arrange(training) results |> select(-oob) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | training| new| optimism| |:------------------------|--------:|----:|--------:| |Decision tree, grown out | 0.00| 6.21| 6.21| |Boosting | 0.02| 4.96| 4.94| |Random forest | 2.23| 4.54| 2.31| |Decision tree, depth 3 | 4.02| 4.93| 0.91| |Linear regression | 4.44| 4.56| 0.12| |Predict the average | | 4.83| |
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def pipeline(model): return Pipeline([("recipe", tree_recipe), ("model", model)]) models = { "Linear regression": lambda: pipeline(LinearRegression()), "Decision tree, depth 3": lambda: pipeline( DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, random_state=123)), "Decision tree, grown out": lambda: pipeline( DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=123)), # oob_score keeps the out-of-bag predictions used further down. "Random forest": lambda: pipeline(RandomForestRegressor( n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, oob_score=True, random_state=123)), "Boosting": lambda: pipeline(GradientBoostingRegressor( n_estimators=500, max_depth=6, learning_rate=0.1, random_state=123)), } rmse = root_mean_squared_error rows = [] for fit_rows, new_rows in splits: fitting, new = train.iloc[fit_rows], train.iloc[new_rows] for name, make in models.items(): fitted = make().fit(fitting[predictors], fitting["abundance"]) forest = fitted["model"] rows.append({ "model": name, "training": rmse(fitting["abundance"], fitted.predict(fitting[predictors])), "new": rmse(new["abundance"], fitted.predict(new[predictors])), "oob": (rmse(fitting["abundance"], forest.oob_prediction_) if name == "Random forest" else np.nan), }) rows.append({"model": "Predict the average", "training": np.nan, "new": rmse(new["abundance"], np.full(len(new), fitting["abundance"].mean()))}) results = (pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby("model", as_index=False).mean() .assign(optimism=lambda d: d["new"] - d["training"]) .sort_values("training", na_position="last") .reset_index(drop=True)) results.drop(columns="oob").round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | training | new | optimism | |:-------------------------|-----------:|------:|-----------:| | Decision tree, grown out | 0 | 5.86 | 5.86 | | Boosting | 0 | 4.67 | 4.67 | | Random forest | 3.23 | 4.22 | 0.99 | | Decision tree, depth 3 | 3.78 | 4.35 | 0.57 | | Linear regression | 3.97 | 4.27 | 0.3 | | Predict the average | nan | 4.53 | nan | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} results |> filter(model != "Predict the average") |> pivot_longer(c(training, new), names_to = "set", values_to = "rmse") |> mutate(set = factor(set, levels = c("training", "new"), labels = c("Fitting stations", "New sites"))) |> ggplot(aes(set, rmse, group = model, colour = model)) + geom_hline(yintercept = baseline, linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2.6) + annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = baseline + 0.25, label = "predict the average", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], size = 3.4) + guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) + labs(x = NULL, y = "RMSE (individuals)", colour = NULL, title = "The order on new sites is not the order on the fitting stations") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Each model's RMSE on the stations it was fitted to and on new sites, averaged over 20 splits of the training sites. Every line rises, but by very different amounts, so the order changes. The dashed line is the error of predicting the fitting stations' average count.](training-versus-new-data_files/figure-html/fig-crossing-1.png){#fig-crossing fig-alt='A slope chart with two positions, training on the left and new sites on the right, and RMSE on the vertical axis. Five lines join each model\'s training error to its error on new sites. The grown-out tree and boosting start at zero and rise steeply; the grown-out tree ends highest of all. The random forest starts at about 2 and rises to the lowest point on the right. The depth-3 tree and linear regression start highest, about 4 to 4.5, and rise gently. A dashed line marks predicting the average, about 5.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: ### The best fits to their own stations do worst on new sites By training error, the grown-out tree comes first with an RMSE of exactly zero, and boosting second at 0.02. Both have fitted their stations almost perfectly. On new sites they are among the worst. The grown-out tree comes last, at 6.21, well above the 4.83 from predicting the average with no inputs at all, and boosting, at 4.96, does no better than that average. Linear regression, last by training error at 4.44, is close to the best on new sites at 4.56, behind only the random forest at 4.54. Only two of the five models beat the baseline: random forest and linear regression. A tree with one station in each leaf predicts every fitting station as that station's own count, so its training error is zero. It has stored the data rather than learned a relationship from it, and the stored counts are mostly noise. ### The out-of-bag error estimates a forest's error on new sites A random forest has a third error to offer. Each of its trees is grown on a bootstrap sample of the fitting stations, which leaves out about a third of them. Predicting each station with only the trees that never saw it gives the **out-of-bag error**, and the forest computes it while it is fitted. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} results |> filter(model == "Random forest") |> select(training, out_of_bag = oob, new) |> mutate(across(everything(), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| training| out_of_bag| new| |--------:|----------:|----:| | 2.23| 4.62| 4.54|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} (results.query("model == 'Random forest'").reset_index(drop=True) [["training", "oob", "new"]].rename(columns={"oob": "out_of_bag"}).round(2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | training | out_of_bag | new | |-----------:|-------------:|------:| | 3.23 | 4.06 | 4.22 | ::: ::: ::: The forest's training error is 2.23, but its out-of-bag error is 4.62, much closer to its 4.54 on new sites. It is not a perfect stand-in, since stations from the same site share a tree's sample, but it costs nothing: when a forest is fitted, its out-of-bag error is the one to quote, not its training error. ### More sites shrink the gap for regression but not for a forest The optimism depends on the amount of data as well as on the model. To see this, each split's fitting sites are cut down to a few at random, from 5 sites to 80, and two models are fitted to them: [polynomial regression](../03-supervised-learning/linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd), with squared depth and temperature, and a random forest. Both use the four measured inputs only, so that a small sample cannot miss a category that the new sites contain. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} measured <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu measured_recipe <- recipe(measured, data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) curve_recipe <- measured_recipe |> step_poly(depth_m, temperature_c, degree = 2, options = list(raw = TRUE)) two_models <- list( "Polynomial regression" = workflow(curve_recipe, linear_reg()), "Random forest" = workflow(measured_recipe, rand_forest(mode = "regression", trees = 300)) ) site_counts <- c(5, 10, 20, 40, 80) by_sites <- map(splits$splits, \(s) { fitting <- analysis(s) new <- assessment(s) map(site_counts, \(n) { some <- fitting |> filter(site_id %in% sample(unique(site_id), n)) imap(two_models, \(w, model) { fitted <- fit(w, some) tibble(model = model, sites = n, training = rmse_vec(some$abundance, predict(fitted, some)$.pred), new = rmse_vec(new$abundance, predict(fitted, new)$.pred)) }) |> list_rbind() }) |> list_rbind() }) |> list_rbind() |> group_by(model, sites) |> summarise(across(c(training, new), mean), .groups = "drop") |> mutate(optimism = new - training) by_sites |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | sites| training| new| optimism| |:---------------------|-----:|--------:|----:|--------:| |Polynomial regression | 5| 3.42| 5.60| 2.18| |Polynomial regression | 10| 3.65| 4.99| 1.34| |Polynomial regression | 20| 4.24| 4.61| 0.37| |Polynomial regression | 40| 4.27| 4.54| 0.27| |Polynomial regression | 80| 4.34| 4.43| 0.09| |Random forest | 5| 2.35| 5.19| 2.84| |Random forest | 10| 2.12| 4.88| 2.76| |Random forest | 20| 2.28| 4.75| 2.48| |Random forest | 40| 2.15| 4.69| 2.54| |Random forest | 80| 2.14| 4.57| 2.44|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} measured = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] def squared(column): return (column, Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)), ]), [column]) two_models = { "Polynomial regression": lambda: Pipeline([ ("recipe", ColumnTransformer([ squared("depth_m"), squared("temperature_c"), ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), ["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]), ])), ("model", LinearRegression())]), "Random forest": lambda: Pipeline([ ("recipe", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("model", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=123))]), } rng = np.random.default_rng(123) rows = [] for fit_rows, new_rows in splits: fitting, new = train.iloc[fit_rows], train.iloc[new_rows] for n in [5, 10, 20, 40, 80]: chosen = rng.choice(fitting["site_id"].unique(), n, replace=False) some = fitting[fitting["site_id"].isin(chosen)] for name, make in two_models.items(): fitted = make().fit(some[measured], some["abundance"]) rows.append({ "model": name, "sites": n, "training": rmse(some["abundance"], fitted.predict(some[measured])), "new": rmse(new["abundance"], fitted.predict(new[measured])), }) by_sites = (pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby(["model", "sites"], as_index=False).mean() .assign(optimism=lambda d: d["new"] - d["training"])) by_sites.round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | sites | training | new | optimism | |:----------------------|--------:|-----------:|------:|-----------:| | Polynomial regression | 5 | 2.8 | 5.67 | 2.87 | | Polynomial regression | 10 | 3.63 | 4.56 | 0.93 | | Polynomial regression | 20 | 3.76 | 4.3 | 0.54 | | Polynomial regression | 40 | 3.96 | 4.2 | 0.24 | | Polynomial regression | 80 | 3.92 | 4.17 | 0.25 | | Random forest | 5 | 3.96 | 4.61 | 0.65 | | Random forest | 10 | 3.43 | 4.47 | 1.03 | | Random forest | 20 | 3.22 | 4.32 | 1.1 | | Random forest | 40 | 3.24 | 4.3 | 1.06 | | Random forest | 80 | 3.09 | 4.25 | 1.16 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} by_sites |> pivot_longer(c(training, new), names_to = "set", values_to = "rmse") |> mutate(set = factor(set, levels = c("training", "new"), labels = c("Fitting stations", "New sites"))) |> ggplot(aes(sites, rmse, colour = set)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 1.8) + facet_wrap(~model) + labs(x = "Fitting sites", y = "RMSE (individuals)", colour = NULL, title = "More sites close the gap for one model but not the other") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![RMSE on the fitting stations and on new sites against the number of fitting sites, averaged over 20 splits. The polynomial model's two errors draw together as sites are added; the forest's stay apart.](training-versus-new-data_files/figure-html/fig-by-sites-1.png){#fig-by-sites fig-alt='Two panels sharing a horizontal axis of fitting sites from 5 to 80. In the polynomial regression panel, the error on new sites starts high at 5 sites and falls quickly, while the training error rises a little, so the two curves meet closely by 40 sites. In the random forest panel, the error on new sites falls slightly and the training error stays flat near 2, so a wide gap remains at every number of sites.' width=1500} ::: ::: ::: With 5 sites, polynomial regression's error on new sites is 2.18 higher than its training error. With 80 sites the gap is 0.09: the model has a fixed number of coefficients, and the more stations they are fitted to, the less noise they can absorb. The forest's gap barely moves, from 2.84 at 5 sites to 2.44 at 80. Its trees split until their leaves hold only a few stations, however many stations there are, so it fits some noise at any sample size and its training error stays low. More data improves the forest on new sites, but its training error never becomes a fair estimate of that. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - **Training error** is a model's error on the data it was fitted to. It is not an estimate of its error on new data and not a basis for choosing between models. - The gap between the two errors is the **optimism**. It grows with the model's flexibility, because a flexible model fits noise as well as signal. - On the survey, the two models that fitted their stations almost perfectly, the grown-out tree and boosting, did no better on new sites than predicting the average count. - A random forest's **out-of-bag error** comes free with the fit and is far closer to its error on new sites than its training error is. - More data shrinks the optimism of a model with a fixed number of coefficients, but not that of a forest, whose leaves stay small however many stations there are. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Change `times = 20` to `times = 5` and re-run. How much do the averages move, and does the order of the five models on new sites stay the same? 2. Give the grown-out tree `min_n = 20` in place of `min_n = 2`, so a node needs 20 stations before it may split. What happens to its training error and to its error on new sites? [The next page](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd) turns this setting into a curve.
